pharm: Long-acting amide local anesthetic that reversibly blocks neuronal sodium channels to produce regional anesthesia and analgesia, with relatively less cardiotoxicity than bupivacaine.
quick: Concentration/dose individualized to block (e.g., 0.2-1% for surgical anesthesia, 0.2% for analgesia); use smallest effective dose
Parenteral regional anesthetic; not related to meals
Used in obstetric anesthesia (epidural for cesarean/labor) when indicated
Limited data; generally compatible with brief peri-procedural exposure
Caution in severe dysfunction; metabolites may accumulate
Caution in advanced liver disease (hepatic metabolism); reduce repeat dosing
Cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs, consciousness, signs of systemic toxicity
summary: Ropivacaine is a long-acting amide local anesthetic indicated in adults for local or regional anesthesia for surgery (epidural block including cesarean section, major nerve block, local infiltration) and for acute pain management (epidural infusion/bolus for postoperative or labor pain, and local infiltration). It must be given by clinicians skilled in managing local anesthetic toxicity, using incremental (fractional) dosing and the smallest effective dose and concentration. Unintended intravascular injection can cause cardiac arrhythmia or arrest, and dose-related systemic toxicity can lead to seizures, acidosis, cardiac arrest, and death; resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion must be immediately available. It is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics and is not approved for intra-articular infusion (risk of chondrolysis).
indications: Local or regional anesthesia for surgery: epidural block for surgery including cesarean section, major nerve block, and local infiltration (adults)
Acute pain management: epidural continuous infusion or intermittent bolus (e.g., postoperative or labor) and local infiltration (adults)

dosage.d: 0.5%, 0.75%, or 1% solutions; dose titrated to block (commonly 15-30 mL of 0.5-1%)
dosage.n: Use incremental dosing; smallest effective dose/concentration

dosage.d: 0.5% or 0.75% solution titrated to block (e.g., 35-50 mL of 0.5%)
dosage.n: Aspirate before and during injection to avoid intravascular dosing

dosage.d: 0.2% solution by infusion (e.g., 6-14 mL/h) or intermittent bolus
0.2% to 0.5% solution titrated to surgical site and maximum dose limits
dosage.n: Respect maximum recommended dose per labeling

admin: Administer only with an IV line in place and resuscitation equipment, oxygen, and lipid emulsion (Intralipid) immediately available
Use incremental (fractional) dosing and avoid rapid injection of large volumes; aspirate before and during injection to detect intravascular/intrathecal placement
Use the smallest dose and concentration required for the desired effect; carefully calculate cumulative dose for infusions
Do NOT use for intra-articular infusion (not approved - risk of chondrolysis)
Continuously monitor cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs and the patient's level of consciousness during and after administration
moa: Ropivacaine is an amide-type local anesthetic that reversibly binds to and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on the internal surface of nerve cell membranes. This prevents the influx of sodium needed for action potential initiation and propagation, blocking nerve conduction and producing localized loss of sensation (and, at higher concentrations, motor block). Its long duration and relatively lower cardiotoxicity compared with bupivacaine relate to its physicochemical properties and S(-)-enantiomer structure.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ropivacaine or to any amide-type local anesthetic
relative: Hypovolemia or severe hemodynamic instability (for major regional blocks)
Partial or complete heart conduction block
Advanced hepatic disease or severe renal dysfunction
Use at injection sites or in conditions where intravascular injection is more likely
monitor: Level of consciousness and CNS toxicity signs

preg: Ropivacaine is used in obstetric regional anesthesia (epidural for cesarean section and labor analgesia) when clinically indicated. As with all local anesthetics, fetal heart rate and maternal hemodynamics should be monitored; paracervical block is not recommended.
lact: There are limited data on ropivacaine in human milk. Given the short peri-procedural exposure and limited oral bioavailability in the infant, brief use is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding.
renal: Use with caution in patients with severe renal dysfunction; while ropivacaine itself is hepatically metabolized, accumulation of metabolites and altered acid-base status may increase toxicity risk with repeated or prolonged dosing.
hepatic: Ropivacaine is metabolized by the liver (CYP1A2 and CYP3A4); patients with advanced liver disease may have reduced clearance. Use cautiously and reduce repeat or continuous dosing to avoid accumulation and systemic toxicity.

major: Other local anesthetics or agents structurally related to amide local anesthetics - additive systemic (CNS and cardiac) toxicity; consider cumulative dose
Class III antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone) - additive cardiac effects; monitor closely
moderate: Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., fluvoxamine) - reduce ropivacaine clearance and increase plasma levels
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) - modest increase in ropivacaine levels
Drugs causing methemoglobinemia (e.g., other local anesthetics, nitrates, dapsone) - additive risk
minor: Vasopressors/oxytocics with vasoconstrictors - hypertensive effects if epinephrine-containing solutions used
interactions.diagnostics: May cause methemoglobinemia (pulse oximetry can be misleadingly normal; confirm with co-oximetry).

serious: Systemic local anesthetic toxicity - CNS excitation (tremors, seizures) then depression
Cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest (especially with unintended intravascular injection)
High/total spinal block, respiratory depression or arrest (unintended subarachnoid injection)
rare: Neurologic injury / persistent sensory or motor deficit
emergency: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (seizures, cardiac arrest) - treat with airway support and IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) rescue

monitoring: Continuous cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs during and after administration
Level of consciousness and early signs of CNS toxicity (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation)
Signs of methemoglobinemia (cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen) - confirm with co-oximetry
Hemodynamics in obstetric and major regional blocks
counsel: This anesthetic is given by your anesthesia team to numb a region for surgery or pain relief
Tell your team if you have ever had a reaction to a numbing medicine (e.g., lidocaine, bupivacaine)
Report ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth, dizziness, a metallic taste, or feeling faint during injection
The numbness and weakness will wear off gradually; protect the numb area from injury until sensation returns
Tell your team about all medicines, especially heart-rhythm drugs and certain antidepressants
pk: Epidural onset approximately 10-30 minutes depending on concentration
Plasma peak depends on site/dose; vascular sites give higher peaks
Terminal half-life approximately 1.8 hours (IV) / longer (~4-7 h) after epidural
Surgical anesthesia and analgesia typically last several hours (long-acting)
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C; protect from freezing; single-use, discard unused portion
pearls: Long-acting amide local anesthetic with a wider cardiac safety margin than bupivacaine, but systemic toxicity (seizures, cardiac arrest) still occurs
Always use incremental (fractional) dosing with aspiration to detect intravascular/intrathecal placement; have resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion ready
IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is the rescue therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity
Not approved for intra-articular infusion - associated with chondrolysis
Watch for methemoglobinemia; pulse oximetry can read falsely normal - confirm with co-oximetry and treat with methylene blue
missed: Ropivacaine is administered by an anesthesia provider as part of a procedure or controlled infusion, not as patient-taken doses; there is no missed-dose schedule. Infusion adjustments are managed by the clinical team to keep the cumulative dose within safe limits.
overdose: Acute emergencies from local anesthetics relate to high plasma levels or unintended intravascular/subarachnoid injection. Discontinue ropivacaine at the first sign of toxicity. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive: secure a patent airway and provide assisted/controlled ventilation with 100% oxygen, support circulation, and treat seizures (e.g., benzodiazepines, small-dose thiopental, or succinylcholine with airway control). For cardiac toxicity/arrest, begin advanced life support and administer IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) rescue; prolonged resuscitation may be required.
